title: Versola
description: Whole-system health: auth, central and edge on one page. Read the Overview matrix first; open a service's rows only for the part that is not green.

panels.title: Pods up
panels.description: Replicas Prometheus can scrape right now. Fewer than expected means a crashed, restarting or unschedulable pod.

panels.title: Requests/s
panels.description: All HTTP requests this service answers, any status.

panels.title: Server errors
panels.description: Share of requests answered 5xx -- the service failing, not the caller erring. Yellow from 0.1%, red from 1%.

panels.title: Latency p99
panels.description: 99 of 100 requests are faster than this, over every endpoint of the service.

panels.title: Refreshes/s
panels.description: Clients exchanging a refresh token for a new access token -- how many sessions are being kept alive.

panels.title: Refresh rejected
panels.description: Share of refresh attempts that were turned down: token expired, revoked, already used, or server error. Users behind these are signed out.

targets.expr: (sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", route=~"/token.grant_type=refresh_token", status_class!="2xx"}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min(sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", route=~"/token.grant_type=refresh_token"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: DB pool
panels.description: Share of database connections checked out. Near 100% requests start queueing for a connection. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: JVM heap used / heap limit on the fullest pod. Sustained near 100% means GC thrashing, then OOM.

panels.description: Auth and edge pulling configuration (clients, resources, forms, locales). If this stops, they are running on stale config.

panels.title: Changes/min

panels.title: Proxied/s
panels.description: Requests edge forwards to protected resources -- the traffic edge exists to carry.

panels.title: Revocation sync lag
panels.description: 0 = the last attempt to refresh the revocation list succeeded. Above 0 = refreshes are failing, and this is how long edge has gone without one: a token revoked in that time is still accepted.

panels.title: DB pool
panels.description: Share of database connections checked out. Near 100% requests start queueing for a connection. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: JVM heap used / heap limit on the fullest pod. Sustained near 100% means GC thrashing, then OOM.

panels.title: Tables without cleanup (count)
panels.description: Tables that have an expires_at column but no cleanup configured: what expires there is never removed. Must be 0. Red as soon as there is one; the list is on the right. A service that does not report it counts as one. No data means neither service is reporting it yet.

targets.expr: sum(max by (app_kubernetes_io_component, table) (cleanup_configured{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component=~"auth|edge"}) == bool 0) + (2 - count(count by (app_kubernetes_io_component) (cleanup_configured{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component=~"auth|edge"})))

panels.title: Which tables have no cleanup
panels.description: Which tables, in which service. Empty when every table with an expiry is cleaned. To fix one, add it to the service's cleanup tables in its config.

panels.title: Requests / s by endpoint
panels.description: Where the traffic goes. `/token?grant_type=…` is split by grant type.

panels.title: Server errors (5xx) / s by endpoint
panels.description: Empty is healthy. Every series here is a bug or an outage of a dependency; the endpoint says where to start.

panels.title: Latency
panels.description: Typical (p50), slow (p95) and worst-case (p99) request. Watch p99 -- averages hide the users who are suffering.

panels.title: Slowest endpoints (p99)
panels.description: The five endpoints with the highest p99. If overall latency rose, this says which endpoint to blame.

targets.expr: topk(5, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, method, route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}[$__rate_interval]))))

panels.title: Client errors (4xx) / s by endpoint
panels.description: Callers sending bad or unauthorized requests. Not an outage, but a sudden jump is a broken client, an expired credential or probing.

targets.expr: sum by (method, route, status) (rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", status_class="4xx"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Requests being served right now
panels.description: In-flight requests per pod. A pod whose line keeps climbing is stuck on something slow; a flat uneven split means poor load balancing.

panels.title: Refreshes / s by result
panels.description: 2xx = new tokens issued. 4xx = refresh refused (expired, revoked, or a refresh token replayed -- compare with revocations on the right). 5xx = our failure.

panels.title: Refresh latency
panels.description: Time to answer a refresh. The dashed line is the 120 ms target for /token.

panels.title: Refresh rejections / s by status
panels.description: Why refreshes fail, by HTTP status. 400/401 are the token being refused; 5xx is the service.

panels.title: Refresh tokens revoked / s
panels.description: Clients and users explicitly revoking a refresh token (logout, 'sign out everywhere'). A spike is followed by rejected refreshes.

panels.title: Token requests / s by grant type
panels.description: authorization_code = a fresh sign-in finishing, refresh_token = an existing session renewing, client_credentials = service-to-service. A healthy system is dominated by refreshes.

panels.title: Token issuance latency p99 by grant type
panels.description: p99 of each token grant. The dashed line is the 120 ms /token target.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", route=~"/token.*"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Authorize requests / s by outcome
panels.description: silent = the user already had a session and went straight through; interactive = the user must sign in; error = the request was rejected (reasons on the right).

panels.title: Authorize errors / s by reason
panels.description: Why /authorize refused. Mostly integration mistakes in a client application (bad redirect URI, missing PKCE, …).

panels.title: Sign-ins started vs completed
panels.description: Users who began signing in vs users who finished. The gap is abandonment and failure -- the conversion of the funnel.

panels.title: Sign-in completion rate
panels.description: Share of started sign-ins that completed. A drop with no traffic change means users are getting stuck -- check the step failures next.

panels.title: Failed attempts by step
panels.description: For each sign-in step (password, OTP, passkey, …), the share of attempts that failed. Points at the factor users trip over.

targets.expr: sum by (step) (rate(auth_conversation_step_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", result="failed"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (step) (rate(auth_conversation_step_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: Edge assertions (DPoP): accepted and rejected
panels.description: Accepted: auth honoured a DPoP-bound token without a proof because an edge vouched for it (the only such path). Rejected: an assertion that did not check out. A few during an edge key rotation are normal; sustained, it is a misconfigured edge or an attack. Accepted should track edge's userinfo calls.

targets.legendFormat: accepted (bound token honoured on edge's word)

panels.title: Edge assertions rejected, share
panels.description: Share of edge assertions refused. Empty when there are none. Above 1% for more than a rotation is worth a look.

panels.title: Hashes waiting for a permit
panels.description: Hashes queued behind the admission semaphore. Non-zero means logins arrive faster than this pod admits them (`argon2.max-concurrent`): add replicas or permits.

panels.title: Permits in use
panels.description: Hashes being computed over the permits the pod has. At 100% CPU no longer follows demand and the queue on the left starts to grow.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (argon2_hashes_in_flight{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}) / clamp_min(max by (pod) (argon2_max_concurrent{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}), 1)

panels.title: Hash wait and hash time (p99)
panels.description: The wait is the part of a login's latency that more replicas remove; the hash itself is the cost of the parameters.

panels.title: Hashes / s
panels.description: Password hashes and verifications completed.

panels.title: auth — Data volume and cleanup of expired rows
Users (approx.)
panels.description: Rows in `users`, approximate: the database's own row estimate, refreshed by autovacuum, not a count.

panels.title: Sessions (approx.)
panels.description: Rows in `sso_sessions`, approximate: the database's own row estimate, refreshed by autovacuum, not a count.

panels.title: Refresh tokens (approx.)
panels.description: Rows in `refresh_tokens`, approximate: the database's own row estimate, refreshed by autovacuum, not a count.

panels.title: Expired rows waiting
panels.description: Rows past their expiry that are still in the database, across every table with an expires_at. Counted up to a cap per table, so a very large backlog reads as at least that. Near 0 is healthy.

panels.title: Data in each table
panels.description: Every table with an expires_at, plus users. Rows is the database's estimate (refreshed by autovacuum). Size is exact and includes the table's indexes. Expired counts rows past their expiry that are still there, up to a cap; empty for a table with no index on expires_at.

panels.title: Expired rows waiting to be removed
panels.description: Is cleanup keeping up? Per table, the rows that should already be gone. A healthy table saws back to near 0 after each run; a line that only climbs is a table cleanup is losing to. Counted up to a cap per table.

panels.title: Live and expired rows
panels.description: How fast is the data growing? Rows still valid against rows past their expiry and not yet removed. Live is the size estimate minus expired, so it is approximate too.

targets.expr: clamp_min(max by (table) (db_table_rows_estimate{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", table=~"sso_sessions|refresh_tokens"}) - on (table) max by (table) (cleanup_expired_rows{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", table=~"sso_sessions|refresh_tokens"}), 0)

panels.title: How overdue the oldest expired row is
panels.description: How long ago the oldest row that should already be gone expired. Unlike the count it has no cap. With cleanup keeping up it stays within about one cleanup interval of the table; a line that keeps climbing is a table whose cleanup has stopped.

panels.title: Rows removed / s
panels.description: How fast cleanup deletes expired rows, per table. Compare with the growth of the table: removal below the expiry rate is a backlog building.

panels.title: Time since the last successful cleanup
panels.description: Per table, how long ago a cleanup batch last succeeded. Resets at each run; a line that keeps climbing past a few cleanup intervals is cleanup stalled or failing (see the service's log).

panels.title: WAL headroom
panels.description: The WAL rate the checkpoint settings allow, divided by the rate now. Below 1× WAL is written faster than max_wal_size / checkpoint_timeout allows: checkpoints start from volume instead of the timer, which writes more full-page images, which is more WAL. 99× means idle. The 1× line is the documented boundary; Postgres can start a checkpoint a little before it, so treat 1–2× as close.

panels.title: Checkpoints on request
panels.description: Share of checkpoints in the selected time range that were started by WAL volume rather than the timer. The aim is 0%; anything else means max_wal_size is too small for the write rate.

targets.expr: max(increase(db_checkpoints_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", type="requested"}[$__range])) / clamp_min(max(increase(db_checkpoints_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", type="timed"}[$__range])) + max(increase(db_checkpoints_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", type="requested"}[$__range])), 1)

panels.title: max_wal_size now
panels.description: The database's current setting.

panels.title: max_wal_size suggested
panels.description: 2 × the peak WAL rate of the last hour × checkpoint_timeout: the rule of thumb in loadgen-runbook/docs/07-wal-tuning.md. Compare with the setting on the left. It is a starting point; it needs disk for that much pg_wal.

panels.title: Idle replication slots
panels.description: Replication slots nothing is reading from. WAL is kept for them without limit, which is the usual way pg_wal fills a disk. Must be 0. Red as soon as there is one; which one and how much it holds is in the graph below.

targets.expr: sum(max by (slot) (db_replication_slot_active{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}) == bool 0) or (max(db_wal_retained_by_slots_bytes{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}) * 0)

panels.title: WAL held by slots
panels.description: The most WAL any one replication slot is holding back from being recycled.

panels.title: WAL written against what checkpoints allow
panels.description: WAL rate against the rate this database's own settings allow. Above the dashed line checkpoints come from volume, not the timer. Raise max_wal_size (see the suggested value above) or checkpoint_timeout.

panels.title: Checkpoints per minute
panels.description: timed = started by checkpoint_timeout, requested = started because WAL reached max_wal_size. Mostly timed is healthy; a rising 'requested' is the same problem as the headroom tile, seen from the other side.

panels.title: Full-page images in the WAL
panels.description: Approximate share of WAL that is whole 8 KiB pages (images x 8 KiB, before compression). A large share is what wal_compression and fewer checkpoints reduce; see loadgen-runbook/docs/07-wal-tuning.md.

panels.title: WAL records / s and bytes per record
panels.description: Record rate from pg_stat_wal and the average record size. Bytes per record rises with full-page images and falls with wal_compression; the rate follows the write load (logins, token rotations). The services publish no per-commit wait metric; the cost of a commit shows in the `Slowest queries` p99 of the database row below.

panels.title: WAL held back by replication slots
panels.description: Per slot. A line that only climbs for a slot with nothing reading it is the disk filling. Drop the slot if its consumer is gone. Empty when the database has no slots.

panels.title: DB pool in use
panels.description: Checked-out connections / pool size, per pool. Pinned at 100% means the pool is the bottleneck, not the database. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

targets.expr: sum by (pool_name) (db_client_connection_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", state="used"}) / clamp_min(sum by (pool_name) (db_client_connection_max{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}), 1)

panels.title: Waiting for a DB connection
panels.description: Time a request spends queued before it even reaches the database (seconds), and how many are queued. Should be ~0; anything visible is added straight to user latency.

panels.title: DB connection timeouts / s
panels.description: Requests that gave up waiting for a database connection (connection-timeout). Empty is healthy; any value is a request that failed because the pool was exhausted for the whole timeout. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

panels.title: Slowest queries (p99)
panels.description: The five slowest database operations by repository and method. First place to look when latency rises but the pool is fine.

targets.expr: topk(5, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, repository, operation) (rate(db_client_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}[$__rate_interval]))))

panels.title: Failed queries / s
panels.description: Database operations that did not succeed. Empty is healthy.

panels.title: Calls to other services — latency p99
panels.description: How long this service waits for each service it calls. Part of our own latency.

panels.title: Calls to other services — in flight
panels.description: Outbound requests in flight per target, including those queued for a pooled connection (the outbound pool). Where the pool is too small this climbs long before CPU or latency averages move; a line pinned at the pool size is the outbound pool being the limit.

panels.title: Calls to other services — failures / s
panels.description: Calls that failed: connection errors or a 5xx from the other side. Empty is healthy.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: CPU cores in use per pod. Compare with the pod's CPU limit: at the limit the pod is throttled and latency climbs.

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: Heap in use against its limit. A sawtooth is normal (GC working); a floor that keeps rising is a leak.

panels.title: Time spent in garbage collection
panels.description: Share of wall-clock time the JVM is paused for GC. Above a few percent the service is starved of memory.

panels.title: Threads
panels.description: Live JVM threads per pod. Unbounded growth is a thread leak.

panels.description: Where the traffic goes. `/token?grant_type=…` is split by grant type.

targets.expr: sum by (method, route, status) (rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="central", status_class="4xx"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Config syncs / s by resource
panels.description: Pulls by auth and edge, per configuration kind. Expect a steady rate per replica of those services.

panels.title: Config sync latency p99
panels.description: How long auth and edge wait for configuration. Slow syncs mean slow propagation of every admin change.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="central", route=~".*/sync"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Config changes / s by endpoint
panels.description: Admin changes by endpoint. A burst here is a deployment or a bulk edit -- expect syncs and cache reloads in auth/edge shortly after.

panels.title: Config changes by result
panels.description: Writes that took effect (2xx) vs refused (4xx: validation, permissions) vs failed (5xx).

panels.title: Notification listener connected
panels.description: 1 = this pod is listening for database change notifications, 0 = it is not and may serve stale config until it reconnects.

panels.title: Notifications received / s

panels.title: Listener trouble / s
panels.description: Reconnects, long stretches without any message, and dropped notifications. Empty is healthy.

panels.description: The same traffic grouped by protected resource (fapi-core, fapi-pay, central, …) -- which API is being used.

panels.title: Where a proxied request spends its time (mean)
panels.description: Average time per proxied request, split into the resource's own answer, the token lookup at auth, and what edge adds on top. The three add up to the proxy latency.

targets.expr: sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/resources/.*"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/resources/.*"}[$__rate_interval])) - sum(rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", peer!~"versola-(auth|central)[:.].*"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/resources/.*"}[$__rate_interval])) - sum(rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", peer=~"versola-auth[:.].*", route="userinfo"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/resources/.*"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Edge overhead (measured)
panels.description: Time edge spends on a request before it reaches the resource: token and DPoP checks, revocation, permissions, rules, the token lookup at auth. The wait for the resource is not included. Measured per request in edge (edge_proxy_overhead_seconds), so p99 here is the real p99. Dashed line: 15 ms budget. Empty until edge runs a build that includes the metric.

panels.title: Edge overhead (estimated from backend latency)
panels.description: What edge adds over calling the backend directly, at the tail (p99) and on average. The mean includes the auth lookup. The dashed line is the 15 ms budget. Excludes /resources/central, which goes through central, not a backend.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/resources/.*"}[$__rate_interval]))) - histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", peer!~"versola-(auth|central)[:.].*"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: edge — Web apps (browser sign-in and sign-out)
Requests / s by endpoint
panels.description: Where the traffic goes. `/token?grant_type=…` is split by grant type. (/login and /complete finish a sign-in; /complete includes a code exchange with auth, so it carries auth's latency)

panels.title: Server errors (5xx) / s by endpoint
panels.description: Empty is healthy. Every series here is a bug or an outage of a dependency; the endpoint says where to start.

panels.title: Latency
panels.description: Typical (p50), slow (p95) and worst-case (p99) request. Watch p99 -- averages hide the users who are suffering.

panels.title: Slowest endpoints (p99)
panels.description: The five endpoints with the highest p99. If overall latency rose, this says which endpoint to blame.

targets.expr: topk(5, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, method, route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/login.*|/complete|/logout.*|/permissions.*"}[$__rate_interval]))))

panels.title: Client errors (4xx) / s by endpoint
panels.description: Callers sending bad or unauthorized requests. Not an outage, but a sudden jump is a broken client, an expired credential or probing.

targets.expr: sum by (method, route, status) (rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/login.*|/complete|/logout.*|/permissions.*", status_class="4xx"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Requests being served right now
panels.description: In-flight requests per pod. A pod whose line keeps climbing is stuck on something slow; a flat uneven split means poor load balancing.

panels.title: Requests / s by endpoint
panels.description: Where the traffic goes. `/token?grant_type=…` is split by grant type. (start and complete = sign-in, token = refresh, revoke = sign-out; a 401 with a DPoP nonce is part of the normal handshake, not a failure)

panels.title: Server errors (5xx) / s by endpoint
panels.description: Empty is healthy. Every series here is a bug or an outage of a dependency; the endpoint says where to start.

targets.expr: sum by (method, route) (rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/native/.*", status_class="5xx"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Latency
panels.description: Typical (p50), slow (p95) and worst-case (p99) request. Watch p99 -- averages hide the users who are suffering.

panels.title: Slowest endpoints (p99)
panels.description: The five endpoints with the highest p99. If overall latency rose, this says which endpoint to blame.

targets.expr: topk(5, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, method, route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/native/.*"}[$__rate_interval]))))

panels.title: Client errors (4xx) / s by endpoint
panels.description: Callers sending bad or unauthorized requests. Not an outage, but a sudden jump is a broken client, an expired credential or probing.

targets.expr: sum by (method, route, status) (rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/native/.*", status_class="4xx"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Requests being served right now
panels.description: In-flight requests per pod. A pod whose line keeps climbing is stuck on something slow; a flat uneven split means poor load balancing.

panels.title: Revoked tokens held in cache
panels.description: Entries in the revocation list edge checks every token against.

panels.title: Revocation sync lag
panels.description: Per pod. Flat at 0 is healthy: the last refresh succeeded. It is only written when a refresh happens, so a non-zero value means refreshes are failing and shows how long the pod has been without one.

panels.title: Revocation list refresh failures / s
panels.description: Any failure means revocations are not reaching edge, and revoked tokens may still be accepted.

panels.title: Replay protection (DPoP) pressure
panels.description: How often the in-memory replay-proof store overflowed. Empty is healthy; sustained values mean it is undersized for the traffic.

panels.title: edge — Data volume and cleanup of expired rows
Sessions (approx.)
panels.description: Rows in `edge_sessions`, approximate: the database's own row estimate, refreshed by autovacuum, not a count.

panels.title: Revocations (approx.)
panels.description: Rows in `revocations`, approximate: the database's own row estimate, refreshed by autovacuum, not a count.

panels.title: Expired rows waiting
panels.description: Rows past their expiry that are still in the database, across every table with an expires_at. Counted up to a cap per table, so a very large backlog reads as at least that. Near 0 is healthy.

panels.title: Data in each table
panels.description: Every table with an expires_at, plus users. Rows is the database's estimate (refreshed by autovacuum). Size is exact and includes the table's indexes. Expired counts rows past their expiry that are still there, up to a cap; empty for a table with no index on expires_at.

panels.title: Expired rows waiting to be removed
panels.description: Is cleanup keeping up? Per table, the rows that should already be gone. A healthy table saws back to near 0 after each run; a line that only climbs is a table cleanup is losing to. Counted up to a cap per table.

panels.title: Live and expired rows
panels.description: How fast is the data growing? Rows still valid against rows past their expiry and not yet removed. Live is the size estimate minus expired, so it is approximate too.

targets.expr: clamp_min(max by (table) (db_table_rows_estimate{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", table=~"edge_sessions|revocations"}) - on (table) max by (table) (cleanup_expired_rows{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", table=~"edge_sessions|revocations"}), 0)

panels.title: How overdue the oldest expired row is
panels.description: How long ago the oldest row that should already be gone expired. Unlike the count it has no cap. With cleanup keeping up it stays within about one cleanup interval of the table; a line that keeps climbing is a table whose cleanup has stopped.

panels.title: Rows removed / s
panels.description: How fast cleanup deletes expired rows, per table. Compare with the growth of the table: removal below the expiry rate is a backlog building.

panels.title: Time since the last successful cleanup
panels.description: Per table, how long ago a cleanup batch last succeeded. Resets at each run; a line that keeps climbing past a few cleanup intervals is cleanup stalled or failing (see the service's log).

panels.title: WAL headroom
panels.description: The WAL rate the checkpoint settings allow, divided by the rate now. Below 1× WAL is written faster than max_wal_size / checkpoint_timeout allows: checkpoints start from volume instead of the timer, which writes more full-page images, which is more WAL. 99× means idle. The 1× line is the documented boundary; Postgres can start a checkpoint a little before it, so treat 1–2× as close.

panels.title: Checkpoints on request
panels.description: Share of checkpoints in the selected time range that were started by WAL volume rather than the timer. The aim is 0%; anything else means max_wal_size is too small for the write rate.

targets.expr: max(increase(db_checkpoints_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", type="requested"}[$__range])) / clamp_min(max(increase(db_checkpoints_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", type="timed"}[$__range])) + max(increase(db_checkpoints_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", type="requested"}[$__range])), 1)

panels.title: max_wal_size now
panels.description: The database's current setting.

panels.title: max_wal_size suggested
panels.description: 2 × the peak WAL rate of the last hour × checkpoint_timeout: the rule of thumb in loadgen-runbook/docs/07-wal-tuning.md. Compare with the setting on the left. It is a starting point; it needs disk for that much pg_wal.

panels.title: Idle replication slots
panels.description: Replication slots nothing is reading from. WAL is kept for them without limit, which is the usual way pg_wal fills a disk. Must be 0. Red as soon as there is one; which one and how much it holds is in the graph below.

targets.expr: sum(max by (slot) (db_replication_slot_active{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge"}) == bool 0) or (max(db_wal_retained_by_slots_bytes{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge"}) * 0)

panels.title: WAL held by slots
panels.description: The most WAL any one replication slot is holding back from being recycled.

panels.title: WAL written against what checkpoints allow
panels.description: WAL rate against the rate this database's own settings allow. Above the dashed line checkpoints come from volume, not the timer. Raise max_wal_size (see the suggested value above) or checkpoint_timeout.

panels.title: Checkpoints per minute
panels.description: timed = started by checkpoint_timeout, requested = started because WAL reached max_wal_size. Mostly timed is healthy; a rising 'requested' is the same problem as the headroom tile, seen from the other side.

panels.title: Full-page images in the WAL
panels.description: Approximate share of WAL that is whole 8 KiB pages (images x 8 KiB, before compression). A large share is what wal_compression and fewer checkpoints reduce; see loadgen-runbook/docs/07-wal-tuning.md.

panels.title: WAL records / s and bytes per record
panels.description: Record rate from pg_stat_wal and the average record size. Bytes per record rises with full-page images and falls with wal_compression; the rate follows the write load (logins, token rotations). The services publish no per-commit wait metric; the cost of a commit shows in the `Slowest queries` p99 of the database row below.

panels.title: WAL held back by replication slots
panels.description: Per slot. A line that only climbs for a slot with nothing reading it is the disk filling. Drop the slot if its consumer is gone. Empty when the database has no slots.

panels.title: DB pool in use
panels.description: Checked-out connections / pool size, per pool. Pinned at 100% means the pool is the bottleneck, not the database. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

targets.expr: sum by (pool_name) (db_client_connection_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", state="used"}) / clamp_min(sum by (pool_name) (db_client_connection_max{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge"}), 1)

panels.title: Waiting for a DB connection
panels.description: Time a request spends queued before it even reaches the database (seconds), and how many are queued. Should be ~0; anything visible is added straight to user latency.

panels.title: DB connection timeouts / s
panels.description: Requests that gave up waiting for a database connection (connection-timeout). Empty is healthy; any value is a request that failed because the pool was exhausted for the whole timeout. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

panels.title: Slowest queries (p99)
panels.description: The five slowest database operations by repository and method. First place to look when latency rises but the pool is fine.

targets.expr: topk(5, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, repository, operation) (rate(db_client_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge"}[$__rate_interval]))))

panels.title: Failed queries / s
panels.description: Database operations that did not succeed. Empty is healthy.

panels.title: Calls to other services — latency p99
panels.description: How long this service waits for each service it calls. Part of our own latency.

panels.title: Calls to other services — in flight
panels.description: Outbound requests in flight per target, including those queued for a pooled connection (the outbound pool). Where the pool is too small this climbs long before CPU or latency averages move; a line pinned at the pool size is the outbound pool being the limit.

panels.title: Calls to other services — failures / s
panels.description: Calls that failed: connection errors or a 5xx from the other side. Empty is healthy.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: CPU cores in use per pod. Compare with the pod's CPU limit: at the limit the pod is throttled and latency climbs.

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: Heap in use against its limit. A sawtooth is normal (GC working); a floor that keeps rising is a leak.

panels.title: Time spent in garbage collection
panels.description: Share of wall-clock time the JVM is paused for GC. Above a few percent the service is starved of memory.

panels.title: Threads
panels.description: Live JVM threads per pod. Unbounded growth is a thread leak.
